Ellenbogen''' (born December 8, 1950) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was an [[offensive line]]man for the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) during the 1976 and 1977 seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[Buffalo Bulls football|Buffalo Bulls]] (1969–1970) and [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech]] (1971–1972). He also played professionally in the [[Seaboard Football League]] (1973), [[World Football League]] (1974–1975) and [[Canadian Football League]] (1978–1979). ==Early life== Ellenbogen was born in [[Glen Cove, New York]], in 1950. He attended [[New Rochelle High School]].{{cite web|title=Bill Ellenbogen|publisher=Sports Reference.com|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|accessdate=February 5, 2024|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/E/ElleBi20.htm}} ==College football== Ellenbogen played [[college football]] for the [[Buffalo Bulls football]]. He was a member of the [[1969 Buffalo Bulls football team|1969]] and [[1970 Buffalo Bulls football team|1970 Buffalo Bulls teams]] that compiled records of 6–3 and 2–9 under head coach [[Bob Deming]]. He played at [[offensive tackle]] in 1969 and was moved to [[defensive end]] in 1970.{{cite news|title=Ellenbogen Aids Buffalo Frosh's Second Victory|newspaper=The Standard-Star|date=October 3, 1968|page=40|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-standard-star-ellenbogen/140330637/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{cite news|title=Deming Still Making Moves|newspaper=The Buffalo News|date=April 22, 1970|page=78|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-deming/140331093/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} When the [[University at Buffalo]] terminated its football program after the 1970 season, Ellenbogen transferred to [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech]] where he played at the [[defensive tackle]] position for the [[1971 Virginia Tech Gobblers football team|1971]] and [[1972 Virginia Tech Gobblers football team|1972 teams]] that compiled records of 4–7 and 6–4–1 under head coach [[Charlie Coffey]].{{cite news|title=Former Buffalo Star Turns Tiger at Tech|newspaper=The World-News|date=October 4, 1972|page=22|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-world-news-ellenbogen/140326633/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} ==Professional football== In 1973, Ellenbogen signed with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]]. During the 1973 preseason, the Chiefs used Ellenbogen as an offensive lineman.{{cite news|title=Pounds on, Not Off Rookie Chance|newspaper=The Kansas City Star|author=Bill Richardson|date=August 10, 1973|page=14|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kansas-city-star-ellenbogen/140326197/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{cite news|title=Tale of UB Gridder's Trail to Pros|newspaper=The Buffalo News|date=August 17, 1973|page=12|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-tale-of-ub-gridders-tr/140332449/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} He was waived by the Chiefs in early September 1973, prior to the start of the regular season.{{cite news|title=Chiefs' Notes|newspaper=The Kansas City Times|date=September 6, 1973|page=1D|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kansas-city-times-chiefs-notes/140332815/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} After being waived by the Chiefs, he played semi-professionally for the [[Albany Metro Mallers]] of the [[Seaboard Football League]] as a defensive lineman, receiving $25 per game.{{cite book|pages=158–165|author=Miller, Stuart|date=2005|publisher=Taylor Trade Publishing|title=Where Have All Our Giants Gone?|isbn=1-58979-266-1}} Ellenbogen was signed by the [[Houston Oilers]] in 1974. He also was selected by the [[Philadelphia Bell]] of the [[World Football League]] (WFL). He requested a release from the Oilers to join the Bell and played with them that season. He spent time with the [[Washington Redskins]] in 1975 but did not make the final roster, later returning to the WFL to play with the [[Shreveport Steamer]] before the league folded.{{cite news|title=To Ellenbogen, Pro Football Is Fun|newspaper=The Shreveport Times|date=September 28, 1975|page=4D|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-to-ellenbogen-pro-football-is/140338701/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} Ellenbogen played on the offensive line for the [[New York Giants]] during the [[1976 New York Giants season|1976]] and [[1977 New York Giants season|1977 seasons]] when the clubs compiled records of 3–11 and 5–9. He appeared in 23 games for the Giants, two of them as a starter.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/09/23/archives/another-shot-at-never-land-for-ellenbogen-giants-giving-another.html|title = Another Shot at 'Never Land' for Ellenbogen|newspaper = The New York Times|date = September 23, 1976}}{{cite news|title='Play Hard, Hope It Works Out'|newspaper=The Buffalo News|author=Jack Etkin|date=November 4, 1978|page=47|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-ellenbogen/140325850/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} Ellenbogen was cut by the Giants prior to the 1978 season and signed with the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]]. He played for the Argonauts for a portion of the 1978 season.{{cite web|title=All-Time CFL Player Roster|publisher=cflapedia.com|date=February 5, 2024|url=https://www.cflapedia.com/players.php}} As his playing career came to an end, ''The Buffalo News'' in November 1978 summarized his career as follows: "Pro football has been a bumpy road for Ellenbogen. '''Bill Nagy''' (born October 26, 1987) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[center (American football)|center]] and [[offensive guard|guard]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]]. He was also a member of the [[Detroit Lions]] of the NFL.

==Early life==
Nagy attended [[Hudson High School (Hudson, Ohio)|Hudson High School]], where he was a three-time all-conference and a two-time all-state selection at [[offensive guard|guard]] in [[American football|football]].{{cn|date=April 2025}} He also earned two letters in [[baseball]] and one in [[basketball]].

He started only three games at [[offensive guard|right guard]] during his first three years at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]. In 2009, he only played in three games after suffering an off the field injury in a [[moped]] accident. As a senior, he started eight of Wisconsin's thirteen games at three different positions ([[offensive guard|guard]], [[center (American football)|center]] and [[tight end]]).

==Professional career==

===Dallas Cowboys===
Nagy was selected in the seventh round (252nd overall) of the [[2011 NFL draft]] by the [[Dallas Cowboys]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 30, 2011 |title=Cowboys close draft with OL Nagy |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/dallas/cowboys/post/_/id/4679689/cowboys-close-draft-with-ol-nagy |access-date=April 30, 2011 |publisher=ESPN}}</ref> After starting four games at [[Guard (American football)|left guard]] in his rookie season, he suffered a fractured ankle while playing against the [[New England Patriots]] and was placed on the [[injured reserve list]] on October 18.

During the first week of [[Training camp (National Football League)|training camp]] in 2012, he suffered a severe sprain on the same ankle he had fractured the previous season. On August 14, he was waived/injured with the intention of placing him on the [[injured reserve list]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Auping |first=Jonathan |title=Two Ankle Injuries Have Defined Nagy's Career With Cowboys |url=http://www.dallascowboys.com/news/2012/08/15/two-ankle-injuries-have-defined-nagy%E2%80%99s-career-cowboys |access-date=August 16, 2012 |website=DallasCowboys.com |publisher=DallasCowboys.com |archive-date=January 29, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129021352/http://www.dallascowboys.com/news/2012/08/15/two-ankle-injuries-have-defined-nagy%E2%80%99s-career-cowboys |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Detroit Lions===
On August 16, 2012, the [[Detroit Lions]] claimed him off waivers, knowing he would have to spend the remainder of the season on the [[injured reserve list]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=O'Hara |first=Mike |date=March 29, 2013 |title=Bill Nagy's unexpected road to Detroit has resulted in big opportunity |publisher=DetroitLions.com |url=http://www.detroitlions.com/news/ohara/article-1/Bill-Nagys-unexpected-road-to-Detroit-has-resulted-in-big-opportunity/0b171a18-fb9f-40cc-8a81-59d40579925b |url-status=dead |access-date=January 22, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160128102108/http://www.detroitlions.com/news/ohara/article-1/Bill-Nagys-unexpected-road-to-Detroit-has-resulted-in-big-opportunity/0b171a18-fb9f-40cc-8a81-59d40579925b |archive-date=January 28, 2016}}</ref> On July 24, 2013, he was released after not being able to recover from his ankle injury.<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 25, 2013 |title=Detroit Lions release oft-injured guard Bill Nagy |publisher=Detroit Free Press |url=http://archive.freep.com/article/20130725/SPORTS01/307250164/detroit%20lions%20bill%20nagy}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Nagy served as a strength and conditioning graduate assistant at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. In 2015, he joined the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin]] football coaching staff.

'''John William Demory Sr.''' (December 1, 1950 – February 14, 2025) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] for the [[New York Jets]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona Wildcats football|Arizona Wildcats]]. After his football career, he became an economics professor at [[Central Arizona College]].

==Football career==
Demory attended the [[University of Arizona]] and played for the [[Arizona Wildcats football|Wildcats]] before playing for the [[New York Jets]] of the NFL,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://tickitytack.wordpress.com/2008/01/20/6-thanks-for-the-demory/ |title=NY Jets #6 – Thanks For The Demory | Jets Among Men |publisher=Tickitytack.wordpress.com |date=2008-01-20 |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> for whom he started three games in weeks 5-7 of the 1973 season.<ref name=where>{{cite web|last=Young |first=Bob |url=http://www.azcentral.com/sports/ua/articles/2009/09/23/20090923whatsupwith0924.html |title=Q&A: Former UA quarterback Bill Demory |publisher=Azcentral.com |date=2009-09-23 |access-date=2014-05-15}}</ref>  In Demory's three starts, the Jets beat the [[New England Patriots]], though Demory was only 1 for 7 on passing, and nonetheless received praise from coach [[Weeb Ewbank]] and the Jets' top quarterback [[Joe Namath]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Will Foster Game Logs|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FostWi20/gamelog/1973/|publisher=Sports Reference|work=Pro Football Reference|accessdate=2022-08-30}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-30|newspaper=The Record|date=October 15, 1973|title=Jets' plan was perfect|author=Rowe, Bob|page=23|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108647868/the-record/}}</ref><ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2002&dat=19731017&id=ZnEuAAAAIBAJ&sjid=sdkFAAAAIBAJ&pg=4140,738125 Amazing Saga of Bill Demory], Beaver County (Pa.) Times, Oct. 18, 1973</ref> and lost to the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] and the [[Denver Broncos]].

==Later life and death==
After football, Demory went to graduate school, receiving an [[M.B.A.]] from the [[University of Iowa]] and an [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] in Economics and Entrepreneurship for Educators from the [[University of Delaware]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.centralaz.edu/Home/Academics/Faculty_Pages/Faculty_Profiles/Bill_Demory.htm |title=Central Arizona College - Bill Demory |publisher=Centralaz.edu |access-date=2013-08-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130507061727/http://centralaz.edu/Home/Academics/Faculty_Pages/Faculty_Profiles/Bill_Demory.htm |archive-date=2013-05-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  He was a professor of economics at [[Central Arizona College]].<ref name=where/>

Demory died from prostate cancer and [[Parkinson's disease]] on February 14, 2025, at the age of 74.<ref name=obit>{{cite news|title=John William Demory, Sr.|date=February 19, 2025|work=AZCentral|url=https://www.azcentral.com/obituaries/pazs1097842|access-date=February 25, 2025}}</ref>

He was selected by the Chargers in the seventh round of the [[1983 NFL draft]]. Elko played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]] and [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]]. ==Early life and college== William Elko was born on December 28, 1959, in [[New York, New York]]. He attended Windber High School in [[Windber, Pennsylvania]].{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/e/elko00200.html | title=Bill Elko | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=26 December 2024}} Elko was a member of the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Sun Devils]] of [[Arizona State University]] from 1978 to 1979 and was a [[letterman (sports)|letterman]] in 1979. He then transferred to play for the [[LSU Tigers football|Tigers]] of [[Louisiana State University]] but was listed as ineligible during his first season there in 1980. He was then a two-year letterman from 1981 to 1982. ==Professional career== Elko was selected by the [[San Diego Chargers]] in the seventh round, with the 192nd overall pick, of the [[1983 NFL draft]]. He officially signed with the team on July 11. He played in 11 games, starting three, during his rookie year in 1983, recording 0.5 sacks and one fumble recovery. He appeared in 15 games, starting 12, for the Chargers in 1984, totaling 1.5 sacks. Elko was moved to offensive line in 1985.{{cite news | url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-08-22-sp-2405-story.html | title=Injuries Scramble Charger Offensive Line | work=[[Los Angeles Times]] | agency=August 22, 1985 | accessdate=26 December 2024 | author=Cobb, Chris}} He was released on August 26, 1985. '''William Elden Kellar''' (born February 8, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]] who played part of one season in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]].

==Early life and college==
Kellar was born in [[Longview, Washington]], but played high school football at [[Hillsboro High School (Oregon)|Hillsboro High School]] in the [[Portland metropolitan area]] where his father was the track coach.<ref name="nfl">{{cite web|title=Bill Kellar|url=http://www.nfl.com/player/billkellar/2518244/profile|website=NFL.com|accessdate=11 April 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref name="oregon live draft">{{cite web|title=2018 NFL Draft: Every Oregon/SW Washington high school player who has been selected, 1936-2017|url=http://www.oregonlive.com/sports/index.ssf/2018/04/nfl_draft_every_oregonsw_washi.html#incart_m-rpt-2|website=OregonLive.com|accessdate=11 April 2018}}</ref><ref name="Cardinal">{{cite news|last1=Keller|first1=Richard|title=Cardinal career overshadowed|url=https://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19771112-01.2.7#|work=The Stanford Daily|issue=5|date=12 November 1977|volume=172S}}</ref> During the 1973 state championship game he scored two receiving touchdowns against Medford, which at the time was the second most in championship game history.<ref>{{cite web|title=OSAA State Championship Football Games, 11-Man Single-Game Records|url=http://www.osaa.org/docs/fbl/history/11ManChampionshipGameRecords.pdf|publisher=Oregon School Activities Association|accessdate=11 April 2018}}</ref> He played [[college football]] at [[Stanford University]] as a wide receiver.<ref name="oregon live draft"/><ref name="Cardinal"/>

==Professional career==
After college, he was selected by the Chiefs in the seventh round of the [[1978 NFL draft]].<ref name="oregon live draft"/> Kellar played five games for Kansas City wearing 82, but did not accumulate any statistics.<ref name="nfl"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Bill Kellar - The Pro Football Archives|url=http://www.profootballarchives.com/playerk/kell00600.html|website=www.profootballarchives.com|accessdate=11 April 2018|archive-date=April 11, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180411111541/http://www.profootballarchives.com/playerk/kell00600.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> He injured his knee in week 6 against Tampa Bay and was placed on [[injured reserve]], missing the remainder of the season.<ref>{{cite news|title=Chiefs injured; two replaced|url=https://archive.org/stream/KSULKSColl197879V85N3265/KSUL_KS%20Coll_1978-79_v85_n32-65_djvu.txt|work=Kansas State Collegian|date=October 11, 1978|page=17}}</ref>

'''William Glenn Houston''' (born August 22, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Jackson State Tigers football|Jackson State Tigers]].

==Early life==
Houston attended Central High School. He enrolled at [[Northwest Mississippi Community College]], where he was a starting [[wide receiver]] from 1969 to 1970.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://nwccrangers.com/sports/2013/4/28/FB_0428131057.aspx | title=Former Rangers in Professional Football | accessdate=February 16, 2019}}</ref> He later transferred to [[Jackson State University]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.naia.org/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=27900&ATCLID=205302072 | title=NAIA Players in the Pros | accessdate=February 16, 2019 | archive-date=February 16, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216094139/http://www.naia.org/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=27900&ATCLID=205302072 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

At the time, he was part of a football program that had future [[NFL]] players [[Walter Payton]], [[Eddie Payton]], [[Robert Brazile]], [[Jackie Slater]], [[Emanuel Zanders]], [[Roscoe Word]] and [[Don Reese]]. Houston was a starter at [[wide receiver]].<ref>{{cite book | last1=Payton | first1=Eddie | last2=Brown | first2=Paul | last3=Wiley | first3=Craig | title=Walter and Me: Standing in the Shadow of Sweetness | publisher=Triumph Books}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Dallas Cowboys===
Houston was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] after the [[1974 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/61719662/ | title=Six Cowboy Veterans Report | accessdate=February 16, 2019}}</ref> He was a backup [[wide receiver]] behind [[Drew Pearson (American football)|Drew Pearson]]. He was waived on September 9, [[1975 NFL season|1975]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/51439765/ | title=Dallas | accessdate=February 16, 2019}}</ref>

===Seattle Seahawks===
On January 23, [[1976 NFL season|1976]], he was signed as a [[free agent]] by the expansion team [[Seattle Seahawks]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/77662936/ | title=Transactions| accessdate=February 16, 2019}}</ref> He was released before the start of the season.

'''William Hill''' (born April 21, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He also was a member of the [[New Jersey Generals]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Rutgers Scarlet Knights football|Rutgers Scarlet Knights]].

==Early life==
Hill attended [[Howell High School (New Jersey)|Howell High School]], where he played football and [[baseball]]. As a sophomore in 1974, he was named the starting [[running back]]. As a senior, he received All-Monmouth honors.

He recorded more than 1,000 rushing yards in three straight seasons, finishing his high school career with 3,147 rushing yards, 228 scored points and a punting average of 41.3 yards.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.app.com/story/sports/high-school/red-zone/2015/11/10/jersey-shore-greatest-running-backs/75444754/ | title=Greatest running backs ever at the Jersey Shore | access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref>

==College career==
Hill accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Virginia]]. He left the school after suffering an injury and enrolled at [[Brookdale Community College]] to focus on playing [[baseball]]. As a sophomore in 1979, he received honorable-mention [[All-American]] honors as an outfielder and was selected by the [[New York Mets]] in the 16th round (#392 overall) of the 1979 Amateur Entry Draft.

After participating one season in the [[New York–Penn League]], he [[Walk-on (sports)|walked-on]] at [[Rutgers University]], to practice football under head coach [[Frank R. Burns]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.brookdalecc.edu/brookdale-athletics-hall-of-fame-class-of-2015/ | title=Brookdale Athletics Hall Of Fame Class of 2015 | date=October 14, 2014 | access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref> In his only season with the team in 1980, he played [[cornerback]], while registering 37 tackles, one interception, one carry for 13 yards and 8 kickoff returns for 177 yards (22.1-yard avg.).

==Professional career==
===Cleveland Browns===
Hill was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[Cleveland Browns]] after the [[1981 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://scarletknights.com/sports/2017/6/11/sports-m-footbl-spec-rel-knights-in-pros-html.aspx | title=Scarlet Knights in the NFL Draft | access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref> He was released before the start of the season.

===New Jersey Generals (USFL)===
On January 15, [[1985 USFL season|1985]], he signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[New Jersey Generals]] of the [[United States Football League]]. He was later released and re-signed on March 21.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/03/21/The-New-Jersey-Generals-rearranged-their-player-roster-Thursday/5598480229200/ | title=The New Jersey Generals rearranged their player roster Thursday... | access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref> He started in some of the games at [[cornerback]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerh/hill00400.html | title=Bill Hill Profile | access-date=February 15, 2020 | archive-date=February 15, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215020301/https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerh/hill00400.html | url-status=dead }}</ref> He didn't get a chance to play in [[1986 USFL season|1986]] after the league folded.

===Dallas Cowboys===
After the [[NFLPA]] strike was declared on the third week of the [[1987 NFL season|1987 season]], those contests were canceled (reducing the 16-game season to 15) and the [[NFL]] decided that the games would be played with replacement players. In September, he was signed to be a part of the [[Dallas Cowboys]] replacement team that was given the mock name "Rhinestone Cowboys" by the media.<ref>{{cite news|title=Who's playing today and for whom|newspaper=Lakeland Ledger|date=October 4, 1987}}</ref> He was the backup at [[cornerback|right cornerback]] behind [[Robert Williams (cornerback)|Robert Williams]] in two games. He started the fifth game against the [[Washington Redskins]] at right cornerback. He was released after the strike ended on October 26.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/10/27/sports/transactions-111087.html | title=Transactions | work=The New York Times | date=October 27, 1987 | access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Hill was a football head coach at [[Toms River High School South]], [[Asbury Park High School]],<ref>{{cite web| url=https://jerseysportszone.com/asbury-park-bishops-2014-preview/ | title=Asbury Park Bishops 2014 Preview | date=August 30, 2014 | access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref> and Howell High School.

'''William Edmond McKoy''' (born July 17, 1948) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] linebacker in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

McKoy was born in [[Winston-Salem, North Carolina]], in 1948. He played [[college football]] for the [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue Boilermakers]].<ref name=PFR/><ref>{{cite news|title=He's a Real 'McKoy'|newspaper=Evansville Press|date=September 28, 1969|page=10C|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108827222/hes-a-real-mckoy/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=McKoy's Smile Not On Game Program|newspaper=The Indianapolis News|date=November 18, 1969|page=27|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108827964/mckoys-smile/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> He was selected by both the [[Associated Press]] and [[United Press International]] as a second-team end on the [[1969 All-Big Ten Conference football team]].<ref>{{cite news|title=No Hawks Named All-Big Ten|newspaper=The Daily Iowan|page=6|date=November 26, 1969|url=http://dailyiowan.lib.uiowa.edu/DI/1969/di1969-11-26.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Bucks Head All-Big Ten|newspaper=Oshkosh Daily Northwestern|date=November 28, 1969|page=16|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/24744248/?terms=phipps%2Badamle%2Bmandich%2Bdierdorf%2Bcurtis%2B%22united%2Bpress%22}}</ref>

He played in the NFL for the [[Denver Broncos]] from 1970 to 1972.<ref name=PFR/> He was traded to the [[Houston Oilers]] in July 1973.<ref>{{cite news|title=Oilers Acquire LB Bill McKoy|newspaper=The Miami Herald|date=July 3, 1970|page=7|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/62787362/bill-mckoy/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>  He did not appear in any NFL games during the 1973 season. In 1974, he played for the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. He appeared in 44 NFL games, nine as a starter.<ref name=PFR>{{cite web|title=Bill McKoy|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|accessdate=November 7, 2020|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McKoBi20.htm}}</ref>

'''William Joseph Frohbose''' (May 20, 1952 - September 3, 2000) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] who played in the [[National Football League]] for one season.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Bill Frohbose Stats|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FrohBi20.htm|access-date=November 20, 2020|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Miami]] and was signed by the [[Detroit Lions]] as an undrafted free agent in 1974. He died on September 3, 2000 as a result of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

==Early life==
Frohbose was a standout [[defensive back]] at [[Archbishop Curley-Notre Dame High School|Archbishop Curley-Notre Dame]] in [[Miami]]. A 1969 graduate, Frohbose was named as one of Miami-Dade's best football players of all time by the [[Miami Herald]] in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bluestein |first=Larry |date=June 25, 2008 |title=Miami-Dade's best football players of all time |url=https://miamiherald.typepad.com/hssports/2008/06/miami-dades-bes.html |access-date=November 20, 2020 |publisher=[[Miami Herald]]}}</ref>

Frohbose went on to play [[college football]] for four seasons at the [[University of Miami]].

==Professional career==
Frohbose signed with the [[Detroit Lions]] as an undrafted free agent following the [[1974 NFL draft]]. Frohbose was activated to Detroit's roster on December 5, and played in the team's final two games of the season against the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Pro‐Transactions |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/12/06/archives/protransactions-baseball-basketball-football-hockey.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=December 6, 1974 |page=52 |access-date=November 20, 2020 }}</ref>

'''William Frank DuLac''' (born January 15, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive guard]] for two seasons with the [[New England Patriots]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Eastern Michigan Eagles football|Eastern Michigan Eagles]].

==Early life==
DuLac was born in [[Detroit, Michigan]]. He went to high school at Bishop Gallagher (Michigan).

==College career==
He went to [[Eastern Michigan University]] for college. He played there from 1970 to 1972.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://emueagles.com/honors/e-club-athletic-hall-of-fame/william-dulac/280|title=William DuLac (2017) - E-Club Athletic Hall Of Fame - Eastern...|website=emueagles.com|accessdate=December 24, 2020}}</ref> He was named team captain in 1972.<ref name="auto"/>

==Professional career==
'''Los Angeles Rams'''

He was selected in the 7th round (167) of the [[1973 NFL draft]] by the [[Los Angeles Rams]]. He did not play for them in 1973.

'''New England Patriots'''

DuLac played for the [[New England Patriots]] from 1974 to 1975.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DuLaBi20.htm|title=Bill DuLac Stats|website=www.pro-football-reference.com|accessdate=December 24, 2020}}</ref> In both years he played 13 games. In his career he played 26 games and started 2 of them. He wore number 68.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerd/dula00200.html|title=Bill DuLac Stats - Pro Football Archives|website=www.profootballarchives.com|accessdate=December 24, 2020}}</ref>

==Later life==
In 2016, he was inducted into the Bishop Gallagher Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gallagherfootballalumni.com/bill-dulac|title=Bill DuLac — Bishop Gallagher Football Alumni|website=www.gallagherfootballalumni.com|accessdate=December 24, 2020}}</ref> In 2017 he was inducted into the Eastern Michigan Hall of Fame.<ref name="auto"/>
